summary: EVPN (RFC 7432) gives intra-subnet connectivity in MPLS and NVO networks. This document defines a new EVPN route type for advertising IP prefixes, for networks that need inter-subnet connectivity for systems that do not run dynamic routing, and gives some use-case examples.

eli5.summary: Not every device can tell routers where it lives. This document adds a new kind of notice that lets the network announce whole groups of addresses for them.

questions: what is an overlay index in evpn
how does evpn advertise ip prefixes

subtitle: A new EVPN route type, RT-5, that lets a data center network advertise whole IP subnets for systems that cannot speak routing protocols.

tldr.problem: EVPN already advertises MAC and IP addresses of individual hosts, but data centers also need to advertise whole subnets that sit behind virtual appliances and other systems that do not run dynamic routing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9136 defines EVPN route type 5 (RT-5), which carries an IP prefix and optionally an Overlay Index (a gateway IP, an Ethernet Segment Identifier or a MAC address) that the receiver resolves recursively to find the egress device.
tldr.outcome: Prefixes are decoupled from MAC advertisements, so a failover such as a floating IP moving between appliances needs one route update instead of thousands, and RFC 7432 procedures stay unchanged.

today: RFC 9136 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2021. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 9135 and builds on RFC 7432.

sections.title: Why EVPN Needs Prefix Routes
sections.content:
EVPN (Ethernet VPN, from RFC 7432) provides Layer 2, or intra-subnet, connectivity in data centers. Together with RFC 9135, this document covers Layer 3, or inter-subnet, connectivity. RFC 9135 describes how the MAC and IP encoded in RT-2 routes populate host routes (/32 or /128) in the IP-VRF, the virtual routing table of an NVE or PE. This document adds the ability to advertise IP prefixes, which gives aggregation instead of one route per host.

Interoperability between EVPN and Layer 3 VPN IP Prefix routes (RFC 4364) is out of scope.

sections.title: The Problem with Existing Routes
sections.content:
Tenant Systems (TSs) in a data center can be virtual machines, or virtual appliances (VAs) such as firewalls, load balancers and NAT devices. VAs forward traffic for subnets and hosts sitting behind them, but they do not necessarily run dynamic routing protocols, so the EVPN NVEs must advertise those routes on their behalf. Some VAs even lack their own IP interface; Layer 2 firewalls are an example.

The RFC defines an Overlay Index as an identifier the ingress NVE needs to forward packets to a subnet or host in a remote subnet. It is a next hop in the overlay address space and can be an IP address, a MAC address or an ESI.

Using the existing RT-2 route for prefixes does not scale. The RFC's example: if 1,000 prefixes are advertised from MAC M2 using RT-2 and the floating IP owner changes from M2 to M3, 1,000 routes are withdrawn and readvertised. With a separate route type, the 1,000 prefixes point at the floating IP, and only one RT-2 changes.

Because RT-5 is a separate route type, the procedures in RFC 7432 do not need to be modified, and an EVPN implementation that does not need IP prefixes can discard them by route type.
sections.eli5: If a toy box has a label on it, moving the whole box is one job. Without the box, you would have to move every toy one by one whenever the box changes shelves.

sections.title: The IP Prefix Route Encoding
sections.content:
RT-5 is route type 5 in the IANA EVPN Route Types registry. A node that does not recognize it ignores it, per RFC 7606, so an NVE that supports RT-5 can still share a broadcast domain with one that does not. NVEs attached to different broadcast domains of the same tenant MUST support RT-5 for proper inter-subnet forwarding.

The NLRI Length field MUST be 34 for IPv4 or 58 for IPv6. The fields are: Route Distinguisher (8 octets), Ethernet Segment Identifier (10 octets), Ethernet Tag ID (4 octets), IP Prefix Length (1 octet), IP Prefix (4 or 16 octets), GW IP Address (4 or 16 octets) and MPLS Label (3 octets). The prefix and gateway address MUST be from the same address family.

  • The ESI MUST be non-zero if it is used as the Overlay Index, and all zero otherwise.
  • The GW IP field MUST be all zero if it is not used as an Overlay Index.
  • The label field holds an MPLS label or a VNI. Senders SHOULD set it to zero when recursive resolution via an Overlay Index is used.
  • The RD, Ethernet Tag ID, prefix length and prefix form the route key.

A route MAY carry the EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community from RFC 9135 to convey a MAC address used as the Overlay Index.
sections.eli5: The route is a form with boxes to fill in: which network, how big, who to ask for directions, and a tag number. Some boxes stay empty when they are not needed.

sections.title: Overlay Indexes and Recursive Resolution
sections.content:
An Overlay Index is an ESI, a tenant-space IP address or a MAC address, used by an NVE as the next hop for a prefix. It always needs recursive resolution on the NVE that installs the RT-5 into an IP-VRF. The NVE can only use the route once it has the supporting route:

  • ESI as index: an RT-1 (auto-discovery per EVI) route for that ESI.
  • GW IP as index: an RT-2 whose IP Address field holds that address.
  • MAC as index: an RT-2 whose MAC Address field holds that MAC.

These supporting routes may arrive before or after the RT-5. If there is no IGP or BGP route to the BGP next hop of an RT-5, BGP MUST NOT install it even if the index resolves. The ESI and GW IP MUST NOT both be non-zero, and such a route SHOULD be treated as withdraw per RFC 7606. A route whose ESI, GW IP, MAC and label are all zero SHOULD also be treated as withdraw.

The indirection gives fast convergence when the object named by the index fails.
sections.eli5: The note says 'ask the janitor where the class went', and then you go find the janitor's latest message. If the class moves, only the janitor's message changes, not every note.

sections.title: Which Overlay Index Applies
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists the allowed combinations of ESI, GW IP, MAC extended community and label, and the Overlay Index that results. A non-zero ESI with a zero GW IP means the ESI is the index. A non-zero GW IP with a zero ESI means the GW IP is the index, and any MAC extended community is ignored. With ESI and GW IP both zero and a non-zero MAC, a zero label means the MAC is the index; with a non-zero label the receiver's local policy chooses between the MAC and none. With only a non-zero label, the index is none, which is the special case for IP-VRF-to-IP-VRF over IP tunnels.

A MAC address must be a valid 6-octet address; broadcast or multicast MACs are invalid and the route MUST be treated as withdraw. With no Overlay Index, the BGP next hop of the RT-5 is the actual next hop and no recursion happens.

sections.title: Use Cases with Overlay Indexes
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four use cases.

  • TS IP address (4.1): the virtual appliances' IP addresses are known, so the GW IP is the index. NVE2 advertises an RT-2 for the appliance and an RT-5 for SN1/24 with GW IP = IP2. If the appliance moves, MAC Mobility applies to the RT-2, while RT-5 prefixes are not subject to MAC Mobility, so the prefixes in the gateways' IP-VRF do not change.
  • Floating IP (4.2): the active appliance owns a floating IP, vIP23, used as the GW IP. On failover the new owner signals with a gratuitous ARP reply, NVE3 issues an RT-2 for M3/vIP23, NVE2 withdraws its RT-2, and no change is made in the IP-VRF table.
  • Bump-in-the-wire (4.3): Layer 2 appliances have no IP address, so an ESI (ESI23) or the appliance MAC is the index. Using an ESI reuses EVPN multihoming mechanisms such as mass withdrawal. The EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community carries the appliance MAC, and the RT-1 for ESI23 supplies the tunnel information.
  • IP-VRF-to-IP-VRF (4.4): prefixes behind an IRB, in a symmetric IRB model, covered in the next section.
sections.eli5: Four stories show how the forwarding clue works: a named helper, a helper who can swap shifts, a helper with no name tag, and offices that talk directly to each other.

sections.title: The Three IP-VRF-to-IP-VRF Models
sections.content:
In this case routing tables (IP-VRFs) on different NVEs and data center gateways are linked directly. The RFC identifies three models.

  • Interface-less: no SBD and no Overlay Index. The RT-5 has GW IP = 0, ESI = 0, and a label or VNI for the IP-VRF. It carries a Route Target for the tenant, optionally a BGP Encapsulation Extended Community, and the EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community, which MUST be sent for Ethernet NVO tunnels and should not be sent for IP NVO tunnels.
  • Interface-ful with SBD IRB: a Supplementary Broadcast Domain (SBD) with no attachment circuits connects the tenant's IP-VRFs through IRB interfaces. The RT-5 carries GW IP = the SBD IRB address and a label that SHOULD be 0, and an RT-2 advertises that IRB's MAC and IP.
  • Interface-ful with unnumbered SBD IRB: like the previous one, but the IRB has only a MAC address. GW IP is 0 and the EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community holds the IRB MAC, which is the Overlay Index resolved to an RT-2 carrying that MAC (with IPL = 0).

Inter-subnet IP multicast is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: Offices can be wired in three ways: straight to each other, through a shared lobby with a street address, or through a lobby with only a door number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7432 apply to forwarding within each broadcast domain, and those of RFC 4364 should also be understood because the two may be used in similar applications.

Unlike RFC 4364, this document does not describe PE/CE route distribution. It treats CEs as tenant systems or virtual appliances that do not run dynamic routing protocols. The RFC calls this a possible security advantage, since routing protocols can be blocked on the NVE/PE attachment circuits so tenants cannot interact with the infrastructure's routing.

When an RT-5 relies on an Overlay Index, any action that filters or modifies the RT-2 or RT-1 routes conveying the index changes how the RT-5 resolves, and therefore how packets reach the remote subnet.
sections.eli5: Since the helpers do not talk to the main office's phone system, they cannot mess with it. But if someone tears up the 'where is the janitor' message, nobody can find the class.
